video_title: Will You Maximize Your Social Security Income? Or Choose Poorly? | Julia Lembcke
gist: CFP Julia Lembcke walks Adam Taggart through Social Security claiming strategy with live software case studies, arguing the decision spans 96 possible months and that the dominant rule is to delay the higher earner (because the survivor keeps only the larger of two checks) while claiming the lower earner's benefit early. She puts trust-fund depletion at 2033 with a 22-23% benefit cut absent Congressional action, walks through the earnings-test trap between 62 and full retirement age, and shows that having both spouses delay to 70 is rarely worth it — roughly $40,000 of lifetime difference even at age 90.

themes.theme: Solvency: the 2033 math and the policy levers

insights.claim: If Congress does nothing, Social Security trust fund reserves are projected to deplete in 2033, after which benefits would be cut roughly 22-23% — leaving 77-78% payable — because ongoing payroll taxes and benefit taxation continue funding the system.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The realistic downside is a 22-23% haircut, not zero — a materially different retirement-planning assumption than the 'it won't be there' framing that drives premature claiming.

insights.claim: Lembcke lists the available policy fixes as raising or eliminating the wage cap, raising the early retirement age from 62 to 63, eliminating the COLA, and means-testing benefits the way Medicare premiums already are.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Means-testing and cap removal are the two levers that would hit high earners directly — a planning risk for anyone building a retirement plan around a full benefit at high income.

insights.claim: The system has been repeatedly patched rather than allowed to fail: delayed retirement credits were introduced in 1972, full retirement age was raised from 65 to 67 in 1983, 50% of benefits became taxable in 1984 and 85% in 1993 — so there is no precedent for Congress doing nothing.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The historical base rate says the adjustment comes through gradual benefit erosion and higher taxation rather than an abrupt cut — which is how the risk should actually be modeled.

insights.claim: The structural problem is demographic: Social Security was created in 1935 when average life expectancy was 61 and there were far more workers than beneficiaries, and that ratio has since inverted.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Frames the shortfall as a permanent demographic condition rather than a funding accident, which is why the fixes are recurring rather than one-time.

insights.claim: The 2026 wage cap is $184,500, so a worker earning $1 million pays the same Social Security tax and receives the same maximum benefit as one earning the cap — making the system progressive in replacement rate.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The cap is the largest single available revenue lever, which is why removing it is the most-discussed fix — and the one with the clearest impact on high earners' effective tax rates.

themes.theme: The claiming decision and its arithmetic

insights.claim: Claiming at 62 delivers 70% of the primary insurance amount — a 30% permanent haircut — while each year of delay between full retirement age 67 and 70 adds roughly 8%, accruing monthly.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The 8% guaranteed annual increase is the benchmark any alternative use of the money must beat — Lembcke's framing is that no market return offers that guaranteed.
insights.quote: where else are you going to find 8 to 10% guaranteed each year that you wait? You can get it in the market, but it's not guaranteed.

insights.claim: Between 62 and full retirement age an earnings test withholds $1 of benefit for every $2 of earned income above $24,480 (2026), so roughly $50,000 of wages eliminates the benefit entirely — and the limit rises to $65,160 in the partial year before turning 67.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The threshold is low enough that most people still working part-time will lose the benefit — the single most common avoidable claiming error.

insights.claim: Withheld earnings-test amounts are repaid after full retirement age through higher monthly payments, but the underlying benefit remains permanently reduced — Taggart's framing, which Lembcke endorses, is that claiming early while working is a zero-interest loan to the government.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart and Julia Lembcke
insights.so_what: Corrects the widespread belief that withheld benefits are simply lost, while showing the repayment doesn't undo the permanent 30% reduction — the reason the strategy is bad regardless.

insights.claim: Lembcke's list of legitimate reasons to claim at 62: terminal illness or serious health condition, being retired and genuinely needing the income, being the lower-earning spouse in an optimized split strategy, or when not claiming would force excessive portfolio withdrawals.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: A checklist that reduces claiming at 62 from a default to a conditional decision — three of the four conditions are objectively testable.

insights.claim: Only Roth IRA distributions, properly-taken life insurance cash value, and return-of-capital distributions (from real estate depreciation or certain ETFs) stay out of modified adjusted gross income — municipal bond interest is explicitly added back for the provisional income calculation.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Municipal bonds do not shelter Social Security taxation despite being federally tax-free — a common and expensive misconception for retirees.

insights.claim: Provisional income is modified AGI plus half of Social Security benefits; above $44,000 for married-filing-jointly, 85% of benefits become taxable as ordinary income, while a benefit is only fully tax-free below $32,000 — so most people watching will be taxed on 85%.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The $44,000 threshold is low enough to be effectively universal for anyone with meaningful retirement assets — plan for 85% inclusion as the base case.

insights.claim: The controlling rule for married couples is that when one spouse dies the survivor keeps only the higher of the two benefits — which is why delaying the higher earner's claim matters far more than optimizing the lower earner's.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: This single rule resolves most claiming decisions: maximize the higher earner's benefit as longevity insurance for the surviving spouse, regardless of joint break-even math.

insights.claim: In Lembcke's first case study — Joe with a $3,500 PIA and Lynn with $1,500, living to 81 and 87 — the optimal outcome is Lynn claiming at 62 and Joe at 70, producing about $1.3 million of lifetime benefits with break-even ages of 80 and 76.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: A concrete template for the most common household configuration — and the break-evens in the mid-to-late 70s are below typical life expectancy, which is what makes delay rational.

insights.claim: Lembcke favors the split strategy on behavioral grounds as much as financial: one spouse claims early and satisfies the fear of the system disappearing, while the other captures the full delayed credit.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Acknowledges that claiming decisions are driven by fear of program insolvency — designing around the emotion rather than arguing against it is what makes the plan stick.

insights.claim: A non-working spouse cannot claim a spousal benefit until the working spouse files, and the spousal benefit maxes out at full retirement age — so in Lembcke's Bruce and Debbie case (both 65, $2,300 PIA), Bruce claiming at 66 gives Debbie $1,200 versus $1,340 if he waits to 70, a gap the extra years of payments more than offset.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Overturns the delay-always heuristic for couples close in age with a non-working spouse: delaying past FRA costs the household because spousal benefits stop growing.

insights.claim: A spouse whose own benefit is less than half the other's primary insurance amount receives an automatic bump when the higher earner files — additional money that does not reduce the higher earner's check.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: A commonly missed uplift for households where one spouse worked intermittently — worth checking against the halfway threshold explicitly.

insights.claim: A divorced spouse married 10 years or longer can claim on an ex-spouse's record decades later — Taggart's mother did so 47 years after divorce — and there is no limit to how many ex-spouses can claim on one worker, which does not reduce anyone else's benefit.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart and Julia Lembcke
insights.so_what: A large, frequently unclaimed benefit for divorced retirees — and one worth screening for in any household with a long prior marriage.

insights.claim: Lembcke reports clients who deliberately do not remarry because their divorced-spouse benefit exceeds what they would receive on a new partner's record — an active behavioral response to the rules.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that benefit rules alter household formation decisions — the kind of second-order effect that policy reforms tend to underestimate.

insights.claim: The restricted application strategy — one spouse claiming a spousal benefit at 66 while their own benefit continued growing to 70 — was closed for anyone born after 1953, an example of Congress shutting loopholes rather than cutting benefits.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Reinforces the pattern that the system is patched through targeted rule changes — so any strategy dependent on a current quirk should be assumed temporary.

insights.claim: In the two-high-earner case (John $3,650 and Candace $3,750 PIA), having both delay to 70 versus claiming at 68 and 69 is worth only about $40,000 of lifetime benefits even assuming both live to 90 — a difference Lembcke calls insignificant once time value of money is applied.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the diminishing return on delay for dual-earner households — the second spouse's delay is close to worthless, which contradicts the standard maximize-both advice.

insights.claim: Lembcke says she never recommends both spouses delay to 70, and deliberately uses average life expectancy (82-83 for men, 84-85 for women at 65) for Social Security analysis even though she stress-tests portfolios to at least age 90 in Monte Carlo work.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: A deliberate asymmetry in assumptions — conservative for portfolio survival, realistic for claiming — that prevents mechanically defaulting every client to age 70.

insights.claim: For wealthy clients where the claiming date barely affects outcomes, Lembcke coordinates the benefit with tax strategy instead — delaying Social Security while Roth conversions and gain harvesting fill up the lower brackets.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Reframes the claiming decision for high-net-worth households as a bracket-management problem — the benefit is a nuisance that crowds out more valuable conversions.

insights.claim: A child disabled before age 22 qualifies for a Disabled Adult Child benefit worth 50% of the higher-earning parent's primary insurance amount, rising to 75% after that parent dies, with the caretaking spouse also eligible — and the family maximum runs to roughly $6,800-7,000 a month.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: The rare case where a high earner should claim at 62 — because filing unlocks up to $7,000 a month of family benefits that don't exist until they do.

insights.claim: The Social Security death benefit is $255 per person, and once the surviving spouse dies non-disabled children receive nothing.
insights.speaker: Julia Lembcke (CFP)
insights.so_what: Confirms Social Security has effectively zero estate value — the entire asset dies with the survivor, which is an argument for spending it and preserving portfolio assets for heirs.
